title: Dialogue across Difference When Power and Conflict Matter
before: Explore how meaning and power shape a discussion, and how to describe agreement and disagreement accurately afterward.

turns.text: Dialogue across Difference When Power and Conflict Matter is for staff who facilitate complex discussions, and for supervisors and managers who support dialogue while carrying real responsibilities. The course looks at how meaning and power shape a conversation, how people can contribute genuinely, and how to describe disagreement honestly instead of manufacturing consent.

The opening case is one many of us will recognize. A team asks community partners for feedback after the outreach approach is already settled. The meeting is warm, but the alternatives are no longer open. So what can the partners actually influence? The course asks us to notice the difference between being welcomed and being able to shape a decision.

Much depends on being clear about what kind of conversation this is. Dialogue helps people explore meanings, reasoning, and possible responses. It doesn’t automatically make a decision or settle a complaint. Explaining what the exchange is for, how input may be used, and which responsibilities stay with the actual process gives everyone a fairer starting point.

Then there are different meanings of respect, where one partner sees a direct question as taking an idea seriously, while another wants time to finish an account before questions begin. The course suggests asking about the meaning and making room for both. Neither preference tells you anything about the quality of the proposal or the person’s character.

Power shows up in ordinary arrangements, too: who sets the question, who controls information, who speaks, and what enters the record. A welcoming tone doesn’t erase those differences, and equal speaking time can help without creating identical authority or establishing agreement. Sometimes the most meaningful contribution challenges the framing of the question itself.

You’ll practice in three situations: two community partners question an outreach draft in different ways, and a facilitator labels one aggressive and the other disengaged. An employee asks why an assignment is judged by rapid meeting responses, and a supervisor hears disrespect. And after engagement, a leader has to describe which concerns changed the work and which didn’t.

The performance example matters because authority is unequal. A facilitator who helps people understand a disagreement isn’t thereby a mediator, investigator, or personnel decision maker. When another responsibility applies, the course says to keep its actual route in place, and no one should have to share personal history or reconcile before that responsibility is addressed.

I find the slide on questions especially practical, because asking “What concern does this option address?” or “What have I misunderstood?” invites correction without asking anyone to explain their biography or defend an identity. Culture briefs can help you prepare questions, but they shouldn’t be used to assign speaking styles. You ask actual participants how they want to contribute.

Then comes the record, because people can understand one another and still prefer different options, and silence, attendance, or a courteous response isn’t consent from everyone. Near the end, you’ll rewrite a closing account that says, “Everyone attended, so everyone approved the outreach plan,” replacing it with one that names input, disagreement, influence, and questions still open.

There’s also a private reflection on your own meaning of disagreement. When does a question feel respectful to you, and when does it feel like a challenge? You can consider another meaning without giving up your own. The aim is an invitation that helps people examine the idea rather than judge the person raising it.

As you begin, think of a recent discussion where views differed, perhaps a team meeting, a partner conversation, or a feedback exchange. What was actually open to influence, and who knew that? Bring that example with you, and notice how clarifying purpose and power might have changed what people were able to contribute.

guidance.title: Power in the arrangements
guidance.text: Power isn’t only about job titles. It’s also in who drafts the question, who received the material ahead of time, and who writes the summary. Those choices can be made with good intentions and still shape whose reasoning enters the record. Making them visible helps participants understand what is open, and helps facilitators notice where a contribution could be lost.

guidance.title: What the record will say
guidance.text: Think about a discussion you might help lead or summarize soon. Before it begins, what could you say about its purpose and what remains open? Afterward, how would you describe the disagreement that remained, and which concern actually changed the work? What would help you avoid presenting attendance or silence as agreement from everyone?
